items.explanation: American agriculture had been depressed through the 1920s and thousands of rural banks failed before 1929, which points to deeper structural weakness behind the Depression. The crash's drama and the suffering that followed it do not establish what caused the decade-long downturn -- and swapping one single cause for another leaves the monocausal reasoning intact.
items.fact_source: 1920s farm crisis and rural bank failures before 1929; unemployment about 25 percent by 1933; Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930).

option_explanations.A: Wrong. A dramatic event is not automatically the cause; the size of the paper losses shows the crash's scale, not what produced the decade-long Depression.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. That the worst suffering followed the crash does not prove the crash caused it -- sequence is not causation, and an effect cannot explain itself.
option_explanations.C: Right. Bank failures and collapsing farm prices before 1929 point to structural weaknesses, weakening the claim that the crash alone caused the Depression.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The tariff deepened the downturn, but replacing one single cause with another keeps the same one-cause reasoning the question is testing.

options: (A) The crash erased billions of dollars of paper wealth within days, the most dramatic financial collapse in American history to that point
(B) Unemployment climbed to about 25 percent by 1933, and the worst suffering followed the crash, which proves the crash caused it
(C) Farm prices had collapsed and thousands of banks had already failed during the 1920s
(D) The Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 collapsed world trade, which proves the tariff -- not the crash -- was the single cause of the Depression
items.stem: A student argues that the October 1929 stock market crash caused the Great Depression. Which additional evidence would most weaken this claim?

items.explanation: The United States rejected the League of Nations and passed neutrality laws, but it also hosted the Washington Naval Conference, arranged European debt payments through the Dawes Plan, and pursued the Good Neighbor Policy. 'Isolationist' captures the avoidance of military alliances but misses the deep economic and diplomatic engagement -- so the label needs qualification, not acceptance on the basis of one decision or rejection on the basis of a confused one.
items.fact_source: Senate rejection of the Treaty of Versailles/League of Nations; Neutrality Acts 1935-37; Washington Naval Conference 1921-22; Dawes Plan 1924; Good Neighbor Policy 1933; United Nations founded 1945.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Senate's rejection of the League was one decision; it does not show the United States withdrew from trade, finance, and diplomacy.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Leaders' speeches about staying out of foreign wars describe their rhetoric, not the full range of what the nation actually did abroad.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The United States never joined the League of Nations -- the Senate rejected it -- and the United Nations was not founded until 1945.
option_explanations.D: Right. Avoiding military alliances coexisted with active trade, loans, and diplomacy, so the label needs qualification.

options: (A) The label is accurate: the Senate's rejection of the League of Nations shows the United States withdrew from world affairs
(B) The label is accurate: American leaders' speeches calling for staying out of foreign wars prove the nation pursued no interests abroad
(C) The label is wrong: the United States joined the United Nations in 1920
(D) The label needs qualification: the United States avoided alliances while staying involved in world trade, finance, and diplomacy.
items.stem: A textbook describes the United States as 'isolationist' between the two world wars. Which statement best evaluates that label?

items.explanation: Executive Order 8802 (1941) opened defense jobs to Black workers, and hundreds of thousands moved into industrial work: real economic gains. But workplaces and the armed forces stayed segregated, so mobilization expanded opportunity within a segregated system rather than ending segregation. A campaign slogan states a goal rather than an outcome, persistent segregation does not erase the job gains, and the 1950s movement's timing does not prove what caused it.
items.fact_source: Executive Order 8802 (June 1941) banning discrimination in defense industries; A. Philip Randolph's March on Washington Movement; Double V campaign; U.S. armed forces segregated until 1948.

option_explanations.A: Right. The evidence shows both change (new jobs and migration) and continuity (segregation), and the claim that mobilization ended segregation cannot survive both halves.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Double V slogan called for victory over racism at home; a campaign's goal is not evidence that the goal was achieved.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Segregated workplaces and a segregated military show discrimination persisted, but hundreds of thousands of new defense jobs were still real gains -- not 'nothing at all.'
option_explanations.D: Wrong. That the civil rights movement followed the war does not prove the war caused it; sequence is not causation.

options: (A) Defense jobs opened to Black workers under Executive Order 8802, but workplaces and the military stayed segregated throughout the war.
(B) The Double V campaign called for victory over fascism abroad and racism at home, which shows Black Americans achieved both victories during the war
(C) Because the armed forces stayed segregated until 1948, the war changed nothing at all for Black Americans
(D) The civil rights movement of the 1950s followed the war, which proves wartime mobilization caused it
items.stem: A historian argues that World War II mobilization ended segregation in American life. Which evidence best evaluates that claim?
Which explanation best accounts for how a stock market crash in New York deepened into a worldwide depression?
options: (A) The Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 single-handedly caused the Depression by destroying American agriculture, bankrupting nearly every American exporter, and cutting off all foreign trade at the exact moment the economy needed it most.
(B) The Federal Reserve caused the Depression by printing too much money throughout the 1920s, which inflated the stock bubble until it finally burst in October 1929.

(C) American loans had financed Europe's postwar recovery, so when the 1929 crash ended U.S. lending, European banks and governments defaulted, and retaliatory tariffs then choked off the trade that might have aided recovery.
(D) Every national economy collapsed because each one depended directly on the prices of Wall Street stocks, so the crash mechanically bankrupted the entire world in a matter of days.
items.explanation: The crash became global through a chain, not a single blow. Under the Dawes Plan, American private loans flowed to Germany, which paid reparations to Britain and France, which repaid war debts to the United States. When the crash dried up American lending, the chain snapped: European banks failed and governments defaulted. The Smoot-Hawley Tariff then deepened the damage by shrinking world trade, but it was one link, not the whole chain.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. This makes one 1930 law the sole cause. The Depression began with the 1929 crash; the tariff deepened it but did not start it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. This reverses the Federal Reserve's actual error. The historical judgment is that the Fed tightened too much and failed to act as a lender of last resort — it did not print excessively.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It traces the actual transmission mechanism — U.S. loans, reparations, war debts, bank failures, then tariff retaliation — step by step.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. This overgeneralizes. Most of the world did not own Wall Street stocks; the depression spread through loans, debts, the gold standard, and collapsing trade, not share prices alone.

items.fact_source: Dawes Plan (1924) loan/reparations/debt chain; Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930); Federal Reserve contraction 1929–33; CED KC-7.9.

items.explanation: Beveridge was selling a policy to people at home, not describing the Philippines. His audience -- senators and voters raised on Anglo-Saxon superiority and missionary duty -- found racial mission and divine trusteeship respectable, so the language turned conquest into duty. Reading the speech as persuasion is what lets a historian use it correctly. (A) mistakes salesmanship for legal procedure -- no law required this language. (C) takes a persuasion piece as a factual report about Filipinos. (D) misidentifies the audience: the speech was aimed at Americans who would vote on annexation, not at Filipinos.
items.fact_source: Beveridge Senate speech, 9 Jan 1900 ('The March of the Flag'); Senate speeches in this debate were aimed at a domestic audience of senators and voters; CED KC-7.2 (imperialist vs. anti-imperialist debate).

option_explanations.A: Wrong. No federal law required racial or religious justifications; treating a senator's rhetoric as a legal requirement mistakes political salesmanship for official procedure.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The speech is a persuasion piece aimed at senators and the American public, and it borrows language -- racial mission, trusteeship under God -- that his audience already found respectable, turning conquest into duty.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. A speech designed to persuade is not a factual report. Beveridge was making a case for annexation, not delivering neutral findings about Filipino society.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The audience that mattered was domestic -- the senators voting on annexation and the voters watching them -- not Filipinos, who had no vote in the Senate debate.

options: (A) Federal law in 1900 required senators to justify acquiring any new territory with racial and religious arguments before the Senate could vote on annexation.
(B) He was speaking to senators and voters steeped in Anglo-Saxon superiority and missionary ideas, which made empire sound like moral duty.
(C) The speech proves that Filipinos were incapable of governing themselves, since Beveridge stated it as fact during an official Senate debate.
(D) Beveridge was mainly trying to persuade Filipinos themselves that American rule would benefit them, since Senate speeches were widely reprinted in the Philippine press.
items.stem: Which factor best explains why Beveridge framed annexation of the Philippines in terms of a racial mission and divine trusteeship?

stimulus.text: "The Philippines are ours forever. ... We will not renounce our part in the mission of our race, trustee, under God, of the civilization of the world." -- Senator Albert J. Beveridge, speech in the U.S. Senate, January 1900

items.stem: A historian argues that the New Deal fundamentally remade the federal government's role in the economy. Which evidence best qualifies that claim?
options: (A) The New Deal changed nothing, because President Hoover had already created the same relief and reform programs on the same scale before 1933.

(B) Unemployment stayed high through the 1930s until wartime mobilization, and farm and domestic workers — disproportionately Black and Latino — were excluded from Social Security and labor protections.

(C) The Supreme Court upheld every major New Deal law without a single exception, which proves the transformation of the federal government's role faced no serious legal, political, or constitutional limits of any kind.
(D) Deficit spending ended the Depression by 1936, showing that the New Deal's transformation of the American economy was complete and permanent.
items.explanation: The New Deal did expand federal power — banking regulation, Social Security, labor rights — but the claim needs limits. Joblessness remained severe until World War II spending, and the era's major programs deliberately left out agricultural and domestic workers, a carve-out that fell hardest on Black and Latino workers. The transformation was real but partial, which is exactly what 'qualify' asks for.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Hoover's Reconstruction Finance Corporation was real but far smaller and aimed at stabilizing banks and businesses, not the direct relief and reform programs of the New Deal.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It concedes the change while naming two real limits: persistent unemployment and the exclusion of farm and domestic workers.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Court struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act (Schechter, 1935) and the Agricultural Adjustment Act (Butler, 1936) — the transformation faced sharp judicial limits.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The economy relapsed into the Roosevelt Recession of 1937–38, and full recovery came with wartime spending, not 1936.

items.fact_source: Unemployment rates 1933–40; Social Security Act exclusions; Schechter Poultry Corp. v. U.S. (1935); U.S. v. Butler (1936); Roosevelt Recession 1937–38; CED KC-7.10.

items.stem: A student argues that America's entry into World War I in 1917 marked the moment the United States first became involved in world affairs beyond the Western Hemisphere. Which evidence most weakens this argument?
options: (A) The United States never used military force outside the Americas at any point before declaring war in 1917.
(B) Americans in 1917 already understood themselves as the permanent leaders of a new global political order, a role the entire nation consciously embraced and never afterward questioned.
(C) Because the League of Nations was created in 1919, American involvement in world affairs must have begun with the 1917 declaration of war.
(D) Decades before 1917, the United States annexed the Philippines, asserted an Open Door in China, and repeatedly landed troops in Caribbean and Central American nations.
items.explanation: 1917 intensified American involvement, but it did not begin it. The Spanish-American War brought the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico under U.S. control in 1898; the Open Door notes (1899–1900) asserted American interests in China; and interventions in Panama, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Nicaragua, and Mexico (Veracruz, 1914) all preceded 1917. The student's 'first moment' claim collapses against this record.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. This is factually backwards — the Philippine-American War (1899–1902) alone disproves it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. This projects a later self-image onto 1917. Most Americans still saw the war as an exceptional crusade; the 1920s brought a return to unilateralism, not permanent global leadership.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. This confuses sequence with origin: because the League followed the war does not mean American involvement started with the war.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It supplies pre-1917 counterexamples on multiple continents, directly contradicting the claim that involvement began in 1917.

items.fact_source: Treaty of Paris (1898); Open Door notes (1899–1900); Panama intervention (1903), Veracruz (1914), Haiti (1915); CED KC-7.15.

items.explanation: Both historians are half right, and the record supports both halves. The same movement that gave voters primaries, initiatives, and direct election of senators also produced disfranchisement constitutions and Jim Crow support, especially in the South. (A) shrinks Progressivism to one cause -- city machines were one target among many, from trusts to child labor. (B) judges 1900s reformers by today's racial standards. (C) overgeneralizes: expanding voting power did not mean the benefits reached everyone equally.
items.fact_source: 17th Amendment (1913); initiative/referendum adoption in western states; Southern disfranchisement constitutions (e.g., Mississippi, 1890); CED KC-7.4.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Corrupt city machines were one progressive target, not the whole cause. The movement also took on trusts, child labor, food safety, and moral crusades -- one cause cannot explain it all.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. This judges 1900s reformers by today's standards. Many progressives accepted or promoted white supremacy; their racial views were typical of their era, not ahead of it.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Giving voters more power did not mean every American shared the benefits equally -- the same era's reforms left Black Southerners and many immigrants out.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It gives each interpretation its due: real democratic reforms alongside real efforts to exclude and control, often by the same people.

options: (A) Progressivism was caused entirely by corrupt city political machines, so every progressive reform aimed only at cleaning up municipal government.
(B) Progressive reformers held the same views on racial equality as modern civil rights activists, so the interpretation of Progressivism as social control must be entirely mistaken.
(C) Because Progressives expanded voting power, their reforms must have benefited all Americans equally, regardless of race or class.
(D) Progressives expanded voting power through primaries, initiatives, and direct election of senators, while many of the same reformers backed disfranchisement and segregation.
items.stem: One historian describes Progressivism as an expansion of democracy; another describes it as a middle-class campaign to impose order on others. Which finding best reconciles the two interpretations?
